claim: Motor learning involves neural circuit modifications in the cerebellar cortex through re-weighting of parallel fiber inputs onto Purkinje cells.
source: Motor learning involves neural circuit modifications in the cerebellar cortex, likely through re-weighting of parallel fiber inputs onto Purkinje cells (PCs).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Ito and Kano, 1982; Ito et al., 1982; Kano et al., 1992; Hansel and Linden, 2000) as referenced in the Introduction.

claim: Climbing fibers instruct synaptic modifications when they excite PCs in conjunction with parallel fiber activity.
source: Climbing fibers instruct these synaptic modifications when they excite PCs in conjunction with parallel fiber activity, a pairing that enhances climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signaling in PC dendrites.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kano et al., 1992; Hansel and Linden, 2000; Coesmans et al., 2004) as referenced in the Introduction.

claim: Climbing fibers spike continuously at 1-2 Hz in vivo.
source: However, climbing fiber activity also occurs regularly at 1–2 Hz (Mukamel et al., 2009; Ozden et al., 2012; De Gruijl et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mukamel et al., 2009; Ozden et al., 2012; De Gruijl et al., 2014).

claim: Inhibitory molecular layer interneurons (MLIs) activated by parallel fibers during practiced movements suppressed parallel fiber enhancement of climbing fiber Ca2+ signaling in PCs.
source: In mice, we found that inhibitory molecular layer interneurons (MLIs), activated by parallel fibers during practiced movements, suppressed parallel fiber enhancement of climbing fiber Ca2+ signaling in PCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging and chemogenetic manipulations presented in Figures 1-3.

claim: Brief parallel fiber stimuli in acute slices produced similar suppression of climbing fiber Ca2+ signaling as observed in vivo.
source: Similar results were obtained in acute slices for brief parallel fiber stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from acute slice recordings presented in Figure 5.

claim: Prolonged parallel fiber excitation revealed latent supralinear Ca2+ signaling.
source: Interestingly, more prolonged parallel fiber excitation revealed latent supralinear Ca2+ signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from acute slice recordings presented in Figure 6.

claim: The balance of parallel fiber and MLI input onto PCs regulates concomitant climbing fiber Ca2+ signaling.
source: Therefore, the balance of parallel fiber and MLI input onto PCs regulates concomitant climbing fiber Ca2+ signaling.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data from both in vivo and ex vivo experiments presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Climbing fibers instruct synaptic alterations by evoking dendritic Ca2+ spikes in PCs in response to adaptive stimuli.
source: Climbing fibers instruct synaptic alterations by evoking dendritic Ca2+ spikes in PCs (Kano et al., 1992; Hansel and Linden, 2000; Coesmans et al., 2004) in response to adaptive stimuli (Simpson and Alley, 1974; Gilbert and Thach, 1977; Medina and Lisberger, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kano et al., 1992; Hansel and Linden, 2000; Coesmans et al., 2004; Simpson and Alley, 1974; Gilbert and Thach, 1977; Medina and Lisberger, 2008).

claim: When activated in conjunction with parallel fibers in ex vivo preparations, climbing fiber-triggered Ca2+ signals in PC dendrites are enhanced in a supralinear manner.
source: When activated in conjunction with parallel fibers in ex vivo preparations, climbing fiber-triggered Ca2+ signals in PC dendrites are enhanced in a supralinear manner (Wang et al., 2000; Otsu et al., 2014; Piochon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Wang et al., 2000; Otsu et al., 2014; Piochon et al., 2016).

claim: Supralinear signaling achieves a threshold level of intracellular Ca2+ elevation that triggers long-term depression (LTD) at parallel fiber-PC synapses.
source: Supralinear signaling achieves a threshold level of intracellular Ca2+ elevation that triggers long-term depression (LTD) at parallel fiber-PC synapses (Finch et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Finch et al., 2012).

claim: PCs receive sensorimotor information transmitted by granule cells during the execution of movements.
source: Certainly, PCs receive sensorimotor information transmitted by granule cells during the execution of movements (Ozden et al., 2012; Wilms and Häusser, 2015; Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Ozden et al., 2012; Wilms and Häusser, 2015; Chen et al., 2017).

claim: Enhanced PC Ca2+ signals are observed in response to externally produced sensory stimuli.
source: Furthermore, enhanced PC Ca2+ signals are observed in response to externally produced sensory stimuli (Najafi et al., 2014a; Najafi et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Najafi et al., 2014a; Najafi et al., 2014b).

claim: Parallel fibers excite molecular layer interneurons (MLIs) driving feed-forward inhibition that can attenuate parallel fiber excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs).
source: To counteract direct parallel fiber excitation of PCs, parallel fibers also excite molecular layer interneurons (MLIs) driving feed-forward inhibition that can attenuate parallel fiber excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) (Brunel et al., 2004; Mittmann et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Brunel et al., 2004; Mittmann et al., 2005).

claim: MLIs can directly reduce climbing fiber-evoked responses.
source: MLIs can also directly reduce climbing fiber-evoked responses (Callaway et al., 1995; Kitamura and Häusser, 2011) and impair LTD at parallel fiber-PC synapses (Ekerot and Kano, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Callaway et al., 1995; Kitamura and Häusser, 2011; Ekerot and Kano, 1985).

claim: During the performance of practiced movements, parallel fiber and climbing fiber co-activity failed to produce supralinear Ca2+ signals.
source: During the performance of practiced movements, we found that parallel fiber and climbing fiber co-activity failed to produce supralinear Ca2+ signals.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging presented in Figure 1.

claim: Disinhibiting the molecular layer through chemogenetic suppression of MLI activity enhanced the amplitude of climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signals in PCs during movements.
source: However, disinhibiting the molecular layer through chemogenetic suppression of MLI activity enhanced the amplitude of climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signals in PCs, specifically during movements when both parallel fibers and MLIs were activated.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging with chemogenetic manipulations presented in Figure 2.

claim: MLI-mediated feed-forward inhibition limits the ability of parallel fiber excitation to produce supralinearity.
source: Quantitative ex-vivo measurements in PC dendrites confirmed that MLI-mediated feed-forward inhibition limits the ability of parallel fiber excitation to produce supralinearity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from acute slice recordings presented in Figure 5.

claim: Bi-directional optogenetic actuation of MLI activity during parallel fiber stimuli altered associative parallel fiber-climbing fiber Ca2+ signaling, dependent on the level of MLI output.
source: Bi-directional optogenetic actuation of MLI activity during parallel fiber stimuli altered associative parallel fiber-climbing fiber Ca2+ signaling, dependent on the level of MLI output.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from acute slice recordings with optogenetic manipulations presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Expert mice reliably produced orofacial movements on command after practice.
source: After practice, expert mice reliably produced orofacial movements on command (Figure 1B; see also Gaffield and Christie, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citation to prior work (Gaffield and Christie, 2017).

claim: During the initiation of licking, the frequency of Ca2+ events in PCs increased nearly five-fold.
source: During the initiation of licking, the frequency of Ca2+ events increased nearly five-fold, indicating engagement of the lateral cerebellum during water consumption (Gaffield et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging and citation to prior work (Gaffield et al., 2016).

claim: Parallel fiber Ca2+ activity closely tracked lick rate.
source: As with MLIs in this region (Gaffield and Christie, 2017), average parallel fiber Ca2+ activity closely tracked lick rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), indicating encoding of licking-related kinematics in their population as observed in other cerebellar lobules (Jelitai et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2017; Giovannucci et al., 2017; Knogler et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and citations to prior work (Gaffield and Christie, 2017; Jelitai et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2017; Giovannucci et al., 2017; Knogler et al., 2017).

claim: There was no difference in the average amplitudes of isolated Ca2+ events in PCs between licking and non-licking behavioral states.
source: Surprisingly, we found no difference in the average amplitudes of isolated Ca2+ events across PCs between these two behavioral states (ΔF/F = 0.223 ± 0.008 and 0.223 ± 0.011, licking and non-licking, respectively; p=0.99; N = 11 mice; paired Student's t-test; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging presented in Figure 1D.

claim: GCaMP6f is sensitive enough to report slight alteration of PC Ca2+ signals evoked by unexpected sensory stimuli.
source: While this Ca2+ indicator is nonlinear (Chen et al., 2013), it has been shown to be sensitive enough to report slight alteration of PC Ca2+ signals evoked by unexpected sensory stimuli (Najafi et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Chen et al., 2013; Najafi et al., 2014b).

claim: The licking-induced activation of MLIs showed a close correspondence to that of parallel fibers during licking.
source: Therefore, it was not surprising that, using in vivo Ca2+ imaging, we found that the licking-induced activation of MLIs showed a close correspondence to that of parallel fibers, measured simultaneously, during licking (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The amplitude of climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ events in PCs did not co-vary with the activity level of MLIs.
source: However, the amplitude of climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ events in PCs did not co-vary with the activity level of MLIs (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3) that increased and decreased in proportion to adjustments in lick rate during water consumption (Gaffield and Christie, 2017).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from dual-color in vivo imaging presented in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Intraperitoneal injection of clozapine-N-oxide (CNO) led to an increase in the amplitude of isolated climbing fiber-evoked dendritic Ca2+ events in PCs relative to control measurements.
source: Intraperitoneal injection of clozapine-N-oxide (CNO), the cognate agonist of hM4d, led to an increase in the amplitude of isolated climbing fiber-evoked dendritic Ca2+ events in PCs relative to control measurements obtained in separate sessions (Figure 2C and F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging with chemogenetic manipulations presented in Figure 2C and F.

claim: The effect of chemogenetic manipulation was conditional, occurring only when MLIs were active during water consumption.
source: Importantly, the effect of this chemogenetic manipulation was conditional, occurring only when MLIs were active. Whereas climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ events were enhanced during the consumption of water, events occurring in the absence of licking movements were unaffected by disinhibition of the molecular layer (Figure 2D and F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging with chemogenetic manipulations presented in Figure 2D and F.

claim: In Kit::Cre mice lacking hM4d expression in MLIs, CNO administration had no effect on Ca2+ event amplitudes during water consumption.
source: In a separate set of experiments performed on a cohort of Kit::Cre mice lacking hM4d expression in MLIs, CNO administration had no effect on Ca2+ event amplitudes during water consumption (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is a control experiment supporting the specificity of the chemogenetic manipulation, with data presented in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Chemogenetic suppression of MLI activity did not affect the rate of Ca2+ events in PCs.
source: The effect of disinhibition on trial-averaged PC Ca2+ activity is likely attributable to an increased amplitude of climbing fiber events because chemogenetic suppression of MLI activity did not affect the rate of Ca2+ events in PCs (1.55 ± 0.19 Hz and 1.51 ± 0.47 Hz for control and CNO, respectively; p=0.51, paired Student's t-test; Figure 2G)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging with chemogenetic manipulations presented in Figure 2G.

claim: Bilateral chemogenetic suppression of MLIs in Crus II slows the rate of licking.
source: Our previous work showed that bilateral chemogenetic suppression of MLIs in Crus II slows the rate of licking, indicating an influence of MLIs on motor output (Gaffield and Christie, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Gaffield and Christie, 2017).

claim: Unilateral expression of hM4d in left Crus II failed to significantly affect average licking dynamics.
source: However, in these current experiments, we limited expression of hM4d to MLIs of left Crus II which, upon suppression by CNO administration, failed to significantly affect average licking dynamics (rate, pattern, rhythmicity, and time from cue presentation to lick initiation; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral measurements presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: More than 70% of identified PC dendrites exceeded a threshold level of altered activity indicative of enhancement during licking movement with MLI activity suppression.
source: More than 70% of identified PC dendrites exceeded a threshold level of altered activity indicative of enhancement during licking movement with MLI activity suppression (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging analysis presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Approximately 66% of the fractional area of all individual dendrites showed enhanced Ca2+ signaling with MLI activity suppression.
source: Next, from these distributions, we used receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves to estimate that ~66% of the fractional area of all individual dendrites showed enhanced Ca2+ signaling with MLI activity suppression (Figure 3C, inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging analysis using ROC curves presented in Figure 3C inset.

claim: After MLI activity suppression by CNO, there was a modest decrease in the inter-branch variability during licking movements.
source: However, after MLI activity suppression by intraperitoneal injection of CNO, there was a modest decrease in the inter-branch variability during licking movements (Figure 3G) that was statistically different (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging analysis presented in Figure 3G and H.

claim: Ca2+ events occurred regularly in climbing fibers with mean rates comparable to the frequency of dendritic events in PCs.
source: Ca2+ events occurred regularly in climbing fibers with mean rates comparable to the frequency of dendritic events in PCs, measured in separate animals (Figure 4B and C), and within the range of previously published PC event rates (Mukamel et al., 2009; Ozden et al., 2012; De Gruijl et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging of climbing fibers presented in Figure 4B and C, and citations to prior work (Mukamel et al., 2009; Ozden et al., 2012; De Gruijl et al., 2014).

claim: The frequency of Ca2+ events in climbing fibers increased at licking onset.
source: The frequency of Ca2+ events in climbing fibers increased at licking onset (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging of climbing fibers presented in Figure 4E.

claim: There was no significant difference between the amplitudes of Ca2+ events in climbing fibers during water consumption versus in the absence of licking.
source: To evaluate whether burst firing in climbing fibers encodes licking-related information, we compared Ca2+ events evoked during water consumption to those occurring in the absence of licking (Figure 4F). The lack of significant differences between the amplitudes of mean events in these conditions (p=0.89; paired Student's t-test) indicates that the spike content of presynaptic bursts in climbing fibers varies independent of practiced movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging of climbing fibers presented in Figure 4F.

claim: Chemogenetic suppression of MLI activity had no effect on climbing fiber Ca2+ event rates or amplitudes.
source: Chemogenetic suppression of MLI activity had no effect on Ca2+ event rates (change of 15.5 ± 16.2% from control, p=0.47, paired Student's t-test) nor did it affect the amplitude of events evoked during licking when MLIs are normally activated (p=0.66, paired Student's t-test; Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging of climbing fibers with chemogenetic manipulations presented in Figure 4G.

claim: Optogenetic suppression of MLI activity prolonged parallel fiber-evoked PSPs in PCs.
source: In whole-cell PC recordings, electrical stimulation of parallel fibers adjacent to the PC dendrite evoked depolarizing post-synaptic potentials (PSPs) that were prolonged when MLI activity was optogenetically prevented with a pulse of blue light coincident with the parallel fiber stimulus (Figure 5B and C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from acute slice recordings with optogenetic manipulations presented in Figure 5B and C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The effect of optogenetic MLI activity suppression on the parallel fiber-evoked PSP integral was indistinguishable from that produced following pharmacological block of GABAA receptor-mediated transmission.
source: The effect of optogenetic MLI activity suppression on the parallel fiber-evoked PSP integral was indistinguishable from that produced following pharmacological block of GABAA receptor-mediated transmission, indicating that GtACR2 completely prevented feed-forward inhibition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from acute slice recordings comparing optogenetic and pharmacological manipulations presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Pairing a brief parallel fiber tetanus with climbing fiber stimulus produced dendritic Ca2+ responses that were no different than the expected summed combination of individual responses.
source: Pairing a brief parallel fiber tetanus in conjunction with the climbing fiber stimulus (50 ms interval) produced dendritic Ca2+ responses that were no different than the expected summed combination of the individual parallel fiber and climbing fiber transients, computed from separately evoked responses on alternate trials (100.5 ± 2.1% of sum; N = 31, p=0.78; paired Student's t-test; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from acute slice recordings presented in Figure 5D.

claim: When feed-forward inhibition was optogenetically suppressed during the parallel fiber tetanus, the amplitude of the climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ transient was greater than the estimated summed response.
source: However, when we optogenetically suppressed feed-forward inhibition during the parallel fiber tetanus in interleaved trials, the amplitude of the climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ transient was greater than the estimated summed response (109.9 ± 2.4% of sum; N = 31; p=0.0003; paired Student's t-test; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from acute slice recordings with optogenetic manipulations presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Enhancement of climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signaling by parallel fibers in the absence of MLI feed-forward inhibition was greatest for short intervals and decayed to non-significance for long intervals.
source: On average, enhancement of climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signaling by parallel fibers in the absence of MLI feed-forward inhibition was greatest for short intervals and decayed to non-significance for long intervals (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from acute slice recordings presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The number of spikelets in the somatic complex spike burst was unaffected by suppression of feed-forward inhibition.
source: The number of spikelets in the somatic complex spike burst was unaffected by suppression of feed-forward inhibition (4.2 ± 0.2 and 4.5 ± 0.3 spikelets; control and with disinhibition, respectively; N = 6; p=0.17; Student's t-test; Figure 5F)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from acute slice recordings presented in Figure 5F.

claim: With a more prolonged parallel fiber tetanus (9 stimuli), conjunctive climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signals were of greater amplitude than the estimated summed responses.
source: With a more prolonged tetanus, conjunctive climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signals were of greater amplitude than the estimated summed responses of parallel fibers and climbing fibers alone (Figure 6B and C; also observed in a matched subset of observations at the same dendritic site: 3 PF stimuli, ΔF/F 101.1 ± 2.5% of expected linear sum; 9 PF stimuli, ΔF/F 114.7 ± 3.6%; p=0.005; N = 14; paired Student's t-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from acute slice recordings presented in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Supralinear Ca2+ signaling was apparent in the majority of PC dendrites examined with a prolonged parallel fiber tetanus.
source: Such supralinear Ca2+ signaling was apparent in the majority of PC dendrites examined, in contrast to that observed in separate PC recordings using a tetanus with fewer parallel fiber stimuli (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from acute slice recordings presented in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Supralinear Ca2+ signaling in PC dendrites evoked by prolonged parallel fiber and climbing fiber conjunctive stimuli was abolished when MLIs were optogenetically activated coincident with the parallel fiber tetanus.
source: Supralinear Ca2+ signaling in PC dendrites evoked by prolonged parallel fiber and climbing fiber conjunctive stimuli (ΔF/F 121.5 ± 5.3% of the expected linear sum of both inputs) was abolished in alternate trials when MLIs were optogenetically activated coincident with the parallel fiber tetanus (98.0 ± 3.5% of summed response; p=0.004; N = 17; paired Student's t-test; Figure 6E and F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from acute slice recordings with optogenetic manipulations presented in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Supralinear climbing fiber Ca2+ signals in PC dendrites were reduced, dependent on the activity level of MLIs during the parallel fiber tetanus.
source: In a subset of experiments, MLI activity was systemically varied during the same recordings using different photostimulus intensities in alternating trials. Supralinear climbing fiber Ca2+ signals in PC dendrites were reduced, dependent on the activity level of MLIs during the parallel fiber tetanus (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from acute slice recordings with graded optogenetic manipulations presented in Figure 6G.

claim: In awake mice engaged in a routine motor task that activates parallel fibers, MLIs enforce normalization of dendritic climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signals matching those occurring spontaneously during quiescence.
source: In awake mice engaged in a routine motor task that activates parallel fibers, MLIs enforce normalization of dendritic climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signals matching those occurring spontaneously during quiescence when parallel fibers are inactive.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging experiments.

claim: Short bursts of parallel fiber stimuli fail to evoke supralinear climbing fiber Ca2+ signals in PCs dendrites due to MLI-mediated feed-forward inhibition that attenuates parallel fiber EPSPs.
source: In ex vivo recordings, short bursts of parallel fiber stimuli fail to evoke supralinear climbing fiber Ca2+ signals in PCs dendrites due to MLI-mediated feed-forward inhibition that attenuates parallel fiber EPSPs.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data from acute slice recordings.

claim: Parallel fiber excitation drives simple spiking in PCs while convergent inhibition from MLIs influences the frequency and regularity of these responses.
source: Parallel fiber excitation drives simple spiking in PCs while convergent inhibition from MLIs influences the frequency and regularity of these responses (Häusser and Clark, 1997; Mittmann et al., 2005; Dizon and Khodakhah, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Häusser and Clark, 1997; Mittmann et al., 2005; Dizon and Khodakhah, 2011).

claim: Climbing fiber-mediated activation of dendritic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels produces local, regenerative spikes in PC dendrites that are subject to amplification by preceding parallel fiber activity.
source: In addition, climbing fiber-mediated activation of dendritic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels produces local, regenerative spikes in PC dendrites that are subject to amplification by preceding parallel fiber activity (Wang et al., 2000; Schmolesky et al., 2002; Otsu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Wang et al., 2000; Schmolesky et al., 2002; Otsu et al., 2014).

claim: Parallel fiber-evoked EPSPs inactivate subthreshold, voltage-gated K+ currents (ISA) in PC dendrites that can facilitate the initiation and propagation of subsequent climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ spikes into spiny branchlets.
source: Parallel fiber-evoked EPSPs inactivate subthreshold, voltage-gated K+ currents (ISA) in PC dendrites that can facilitate the initiation and propagation of subsequent climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ spikes into spiny branchlets, thereby enhancing intracellular Ca2+ entry (Otsu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Otsu et al., 2014).

claim: The sensitivity of climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signaling to enhancement by parallel fibers could be restored by longer lasting parallel fiber stimuli.
source: However, in our acute slice experiments, the sensitivity of climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signaling to enhancement by parallel fibers could be restored by longer lasting parallel fiber stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from acute slice recordings presented in Figure 6.

claim: Ca2+ signals produced in the PC dendrite by climbing fiber excitation are a biochemical trigger for inducing synaptic plasticity.
source: Ca2+ signals produced in the PC dendrite by climbing fiber excitation have been subject to intensive investigation because intracellular Ca2+ elevation is a biochemical trigger for inducing synaptic plasticity (Finch et al., 2012; Lamont and Weber, 2012), and synaptic plasticity has been implicated as a neural correlate of motor learning and memory (Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971; Ito and Kano, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Finch et al., 2012; Lamont and Weber, 2012; Marr, 1969; Albus, 1971; Ito and Kano, 1982).

claim: When activated alone, climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signals are insufficient to induce synaptic re-weighting of parallel fiber-PC synapses.
source: When activated alone, climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signals are insufficient to induce synaptic re-weighting of parallel fiber-PC synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about cerebellar plasticity mechanisms.

claim: Amplification of climbing fiber signals by preceding parallel fiber activity can achieve a threshold level of Ca2+ elevation necessary to generate short- and long-term plasticity at parallel fiber inputs.
source: However, amplification of climbing fiber signals by preceding parallel fiber activity can achieve a threshold level of Ca2+ elevation necessary to generate short- and long-term plasticity at parallel fiber inputs (Wang et al., 2000; Brenowitz and Regehr, 2005; Tanaka et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Wang et al., 2000; Brenowitz and Regehr, 2005; Tanaka et al., 2007).

claim: By preventing parallel fiber enhancement of Ca2+ signaling, MLI-mediated inhibition may suppress the induction of climbing fiber-mediated plasticity despite the interaction of these two inputs.
source: Therefore, by preventing parallel fiber enhancement of Ca2+ signaling, MLI-mediated inhibition may suppress the induction of climbing fiber-mediated plasticity despite the interaction of these two inputs.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Genetic deletion of GABAARs from PCs impedes consolidation of motor learning.
source: Interestingly, genetic deletion of GABAARs from PCs impedes consolidation of motor learning (Wulff et al., 2009), a result that may be attributable to the disinhibition of PCs and indiscriminate plasticity produced by unregulated, supralinear climbing fiber Ca2+ signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Wulff et al., 2009) and inference about the mechanism.

claim: Interneurons in the cortex, hippocampus, amygdala, and striatum dynamically regulate dendritic processing in their postsynaptic targets.
source: Interneurons in the cortex, hippocampus, amygdala, and striatum are known to dynamically regulate dendritic processing in their postsynaptic targets, electrogenically gating synaptic interactions that lead to alterations in circuit function (Paulsen and Moser, 1998; Letzkus et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Paulsen and Moser, 1998; Letzkus et al., 2015).

claim: During behavior, MLIs exert a widespread suppression of supralinear climbing fiber Ca2+ signaling throughout the PC dendrite.
source: Although inhibition can elicit branch-and synapse-specific control of Ca2+ signaling (Callaway et al., 1995; Chiu et al., 2013), our results indicate that during behavior, MLIs exert a widespread suppression of supralinear climbing fiber Ca2+ signaling throughout the PC dendrite, perhaps owing to the highly coherent activation of their ensemble during orofacial movements (Astorga et al., 2017; Gaffield and Christie, 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion of the study supported by experimental data and citations to prior work (Callaway et al., 1995; Chiu et al., 2013; Astorga et al., 2017; Gaffield and Christie, 2017).

claim: Ca2+ responses in PC dendrites are not always augmented by the context of active motor behavior.
source: A novel aspect of our findings is that Ca2+ responses in PC dendrites are not always augmented by the context of active motor behavior.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data from in vivo imaging.

claim: Climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ activity increases in PCs at the onset of water consumption.
source: During these trials, as well as during un-cued licking with free access to water, climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ activity increases in PCs at the onset of water consumption (Gaffield et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Gaffield et al., 2016).

claim: External sensory cues that can guide associative learning evoke graded climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signals in PC dendrites.
source: This hypothesis is consistent with work showing that external sensory cues that can guide associative learning (e.g., classical eyeblink conditioning), evoke graded climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signals in PC dendrites (Najafi et al., 2014a; Najafi et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Najafi et al., 2014a; Najafi et al., 2014b).

claim: Spike bursting of granule cells could shift the balance of parallel fiber excitation and feed-forward inhibition through short-term plasticity.
source: Spike bursting of granule cells could shift the balance of parallel fiber excitation and feed-forward inhibition through short-term plasticity (Häusser and Clark, 1997; Grangeray-Vilmint et al., 2018), perhaps unlocking the ability of parallel fibers to generate non-linear Ca2+ signaling in PCs when activated by multimodal streams of sensorimotor information, as occurs during associative learning (Chadderton et al., 2004; Ishikawa et al., 2015; Giovannucci et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to prior work (Häusser and Clark, 1997; Grangeray-Vilmint et al., 2018; Chadderton et al., 2004; Ishikawa et al., 2015; Giovannucci et al., 2017).

claim: MLIs inhibit one another through their structured GABAergic interconnections.
source: In addition, MLIs inhibit one another through their structured GABAergic interconnections (Kim et al., 2014; Rieubland et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kim et al., 2014; Rieubland et al., 2014).

claim: By gating supralinear climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signaling, molecular layer inhibition may prevent unwarranted or unnecessary adaptation during accurately performed movements.
source: By gating supralinear climbing fiber-evoked Ca2+ signaling, molecular layer inhibition may prevent unwarranted or unnecessary adaptation during accurately performed movements.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study inferred from the experimental findings.
